en: I behold the compassionate Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti, who dwells on the slope of the banyan tree; his lotus-face shines with a gentle smile, his divine form is more beautiful than hundreds of millions of Cupids, and his slender crescent moon is entwined within his soft, slightly reddish matted locks. 1.

Salutations to that Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti, the embodiment of the venerable Guru. To him who, like a great yogin or a master of illusion, by his own will causes this world—which was previously free from conceptualization, like a sprout within a seed—to gradually unfold, variegated by the diversity of the mental constructions of space and time fashioned by *māyā*; salutations to him... 2–3. To that Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti, the embodiment of the venerable Guru, be this salutation.

Salutations to Him whose vibration, being of the nature of existence, shines forth as the unreal world of effects, and who, through the Vedic word "That thou art," directly awakens those who have taken refuge in Him;
by the direct realization of Him, there shall be no more returning to the ocean of worldly existence.
Salutations to Him whose knowledge—brilliant like the light of a great lamp situated within a jar with many holes—pulsates outward through the doors of the senses, such as the eyes.
I know that very one who is the witness of all this entire world; to Him... 5.

Those who speak excessively, deluded by the notion of "I am," consider the body, the vital breath, the senses, and even the flickering intellect to be empty, like women, children, the blind, or the dull-witted; to Him who destroys the great delusion fashioned by the play of the power of Māyā...
6. To Him who destroys the great delusion fashioned by the play of the power of Māyā...

To Him who, like the sun or moon eclipsed by Rāhu, becomes the pure existence (sanmātra) through the withdrawal of the instruments due to the concealment of Māyā, and who, having become the person in deep sleep, is recognized at the time of awakening by the thought "I slept before"; and who, though all states such as childhood, waking, and so forth have receded, remains ever-shining within as the "I" persisting even through them... 7 [And] who, likewise, persists throughout all changing states—even in childhood and the like, and in the waking state and so on—shining constantly as the innermost "I"... 7b.
To him who reveals his own self to those who worship him with the auspicious *mudrā*...

8 He who perceives the universe through the relationship of cause and effect, through the relationship of master and servant, likewise through the relationship of disciple and teacher, and similarly through distinctions such as father and son;
he who is this Puruṣa, deluded by Māyā whether in dream or in waking—salutations to him! 9
To Him from whom this entire universe—consisting of the moving and the non-moving—appears as His very own eightfold form: Earth, Water, Fire, Air, Ether, the Sun, the Moon, and the Spirit;
and for those who investigate, nothing else whatsoever exists apart from that Supreme Lord—to Him [be salutation].

Because this "state of being the Self of all" has been clearly demonstrated in this hymn of praise, therefore, by hearing it, by reflecting upon its meaning, by meditating on it, and by reciting it aloud—

May the state of lordship, accompanied by the great power of being the self of all, be spontaneously established; and may that unimpeded sovereignty, which has further transformed into eightfold forms, be attained.

(11) I bow down from afar to the Lord Dakṣiṇāmūrti, the teacher of the three worlds, who is seated upon a patch of ground near a banyan tree, bestowing knowledge upon all the sages, and who is expert at cutting asunder the suffering of birth and death. (12)
A wondrous sight at the foot of the banyan tree: the disciples are aged and the teacher is young;
yet the silence of the teacher is his exposition, and the disciples have their doubts severed.

I bow to the Lord of Teachers, the embodiment of bliss, who has revealed the reality of the Supreme Brahman through the exposition of silence; who is surrounded by a multitude of youthful sages and most venerable disciples established in Brahman; and who holds the mudrā of consciousness in his hand.
I praise Dakṣiṇāmūrti, who delights in his own self and possesses a joyful countenance.

I praise the King of Gurus, the primordial embodiment of bliss, whose sole nature is the happiness of perfectly pure knowledge, who is the cause of wisdom and bestows the ultimate truth, sporting in the ocean of consciousness.
Within whom there is neither beginning nor middle, nor hands and feet, nor name, nor lineage, nor scripture;
who has no birth, no caste, and no color; who is neither male, nor neuter, nor female;
who has neither form nor shape, and for whom there is neither birth nor death, nor merit nor sin.
That reality is our single reality, the innate state of equal flavor; I bow to that true Guru.
(16) Enough with conceptual constructions! I alone am the absolute; this entire universe, moving and unmoving, abides within me.
He who has revealed this secret to me is indeed the Guru alone, worthy of my salutation. (17)
Thus ends the Dakṣiṇāmūrtyaṣṭaka composed by the venerable Śaṅkarācārya.
